html:
Silver coins struck on the island of Aegina, in the Saronic Gulf near Athens, from around the middle of the 6th century BCE, stamped with a sea turtle. They are among the earliest coins of mainland Greece.

Coins had been invented a little earlier in Lydia, in Asia Minor. Aegina was a trading island with a large merchant fleet, and its coins, called staters, spread fast. Their weight became the Aeginetan standard, used across the Peloponnese, Crete and the Cyclades, a rival to the lighter Attic standard of Athens.

Around the middle of the 5th century the sea turtle was replaced by a land tortoise, a change many link to Aegina's defeat by Athens. Athens' owl coins, made from the silver of Laurion, then became the most trusted money in the Aegean. Aegina's wealth in this age also paid for the Temple of Aphaia.
sum: Silver coins struck on the island of Aegina, in the Saronic Gulf near Athens, from around the middle of the 6th century BCE, stamped with a sea turtle. They are among the earliest coins of mainland Greece.
